papers.title: AI-assisted divergent pedagogy: Understanding human-AI co-creativity in design thinking education
papers.abstract: This research examines how generative artificial intelligence (AI) participates in students' judgement practices within a design thinking class. Drawing on 35 design portfolios from a third-year interaction design course in New Zealand, the study examines students' engagement with generative tools across the stages of design thinking. Through thematic and cross-case analysis, the research identifies a recurrent feedback-driven generative loop in which generation, comparison, and revision form the basic unit of activity. Rather than functioning as an external aid, AI is documented in the portfolios as a form of generative mediation that participates in how generation, comparison, and revision unfold across the design process. Empirical analysis indicates multiple modes through which generative feedback is associated with problem framing, divergent trajectories, strategic adjustment, and boundary negotiation. Students' practices demonstrate how iterative prompting, cross-platform orchestration, and reflective correction situate AI within evolving judgement cycles. Building on theories of design cognition and distributed cognition, the paper proposes the framework of AI-assisted Divergent Pedagogy as a process-oriented interpretive approach for examining how generative feedback repeatedly enters design processes under specific pedagogical conditions.

papers.title: The venture clienting readiness canvas: How corporations can assess their organizational readiness for VCL
papers.abstract: Venture clienting (VCL) emerged as an increasingly prominent form of collaboration between corporations and new ventures. However, many VCL initiatives stall because corporations are not organizationally prepared to collaborate with new ventures. Using a design science (DS) methodology, this study introduces the Venture Clienting Readiness Canvas, an ex-ante assessment tool that helps corporations evaluate the internal conditions necessary for successful VCL before engagement begins. We derived five readiness domains—strategic alignment, collaboration governance, communication and trust, organizational culture, and collaboration processes—from a systematic literature review. In addition, we refined the canvas through four practitioner workshops with experienced VCL experts as part of a formative evaluation and subsequently assessed the artifact in a summative evaluation involving nine additional VCL practitioners. The results demonstrate that the canvas offers a structured, actionable approach to assessing organizational readiness for VCL. Thus, this study contributes prescriptive design knowledge on how corporations can anticipate the organizational tensions, coordination demands, and organizational change necessities inherent in collaborating with new ventures.

papers.title: Reconciling disciplinary contradiction in interdisciplinary design projects: A case study of developing a Total Artificial Heart Controller
papers.abstract: Interdisciplinary design's benefits are well documented, yet its challenges are typically framed as communication or knowledge translation issues between experts during a project. In highly regulated contexts such as medical device design, these extend beyond communication to include fundamentally opposing priorities and ways of working. This paper presents a longitudinal case study on the redesign of a Total Artificial Heart Controller. The collaboration was analysed through three broad dialectical oppositions and 22 sub contradictions synthesised from existing literature. It illustrates how mapping specific contradictions (e.g. profit versus novelty) before the design work begins allows them to be operationalised as creative constraints rather than points of conflict. Whereas traditional approaches treat disciplinary difference reactively, this study demonstrates a methodological approach for anticipatory reconciliation. This approach reduces post-hoc negotiation burdens, streamlines interdisciplinary collaboration, enables design contributions that would otherwise be marginalised in regulatory environments, and provides designers with a structured way to align emotional, experiential and technical aims. Nine transferable design principles are provided that operationalise this approach for other regulated interdisciplinary projects.

papers.title: Advancing healthcare foresight: insights from the 'National Ambulance Service 2040' project
papers.abstract: Healthcare systems face escalating long-term uncertainty due to technological advancement, demographic shifts, and heightened social demands, yet foresight is still insufficiently employed within mission-critical healthcare institutions. This article contributes to futures studies by providing a comprehensive empirical case of applied, participatory, and normative foresight conducted within a national ambulance service. Drawing on the 'National Ambulance Service 2040' project in Hungary, the findings indicate how classic foresight methods – STEEP analysis, scenario development, future workshops – can be adapted and combined in the context of a mission-critical public institution.

papers.title: A Processual Model of Artifact-Mediated Controversy in Public Speculative Design
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes socio-technical systems, engaging the public in reflecting on alternative futures is increasingly critical. While Speculative Design mobilizes provocative artifacts to stimulate critique, artifacts are often treated as representational outcomes rather than mediators within public engagement. Drawing on empirical data from a four-month project involving 42 design students who engaged diverse publics through online and offline formats, we examine how speculative artifacts were interpreted, contested, and reconfigured over time.

papers.title: A meta-analytic study on the relationship between service innovation and firm performance
papers.journal: Journal of Service Theory and Practice
papers.abstract: This study aims to identify conditions under which service innovation is positively or negatively related to firm performance. Based on Teece's (1986) profiting from innovation (PFI) framework, the present study examined the moderating effects of the degree of service economy, technological turbulence, market orientation, frontline employee commitment, leadership, and learning orientation between service innovation and firm performance. Specifically, this study conducted meta-analytic research on 198 independent samples from 72 studies via meta-regression and fsQCA.

papers.title: An empirics-first approach to problem formulation in service research: an illustration using the Cynefin framework
papers.abstract: Although service research is an applied discipline, much of the field has emphasized confirmatory inquiry in relatively ordered settings. While such research remains valuable, it is often less well suited to emerging, relational and poorly understood service phenomena. This article therefore argues for an empirics-first approach to problem formulation in service research. Drawing on the Cynefin framework, the article distinguishes among clear, complicated, complex and chaotic service problems.
papers.summary_ja: Cynefinフレームワークを用いてサービス研究における問題の複雑性を識別し、新興・関係性・不明確なサービス現象には確認的調査より「実証優先アプローチ」を適用すべきと論じる概念論文。
papers.analysis_unit: 概念論文（Cynefinフレームワークに基づく問題設定アプローチの提案）

papers.title: Living Artifacts In Design Science Research: Data-Driven Design And Evaluation In Use
papers.journal: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
papers.abstract: Design science research (DSR) increasingly addresses digital artifacts that do not stabilize at deployment but continue to evolve in use. Such artifacts generate digital trace data that make their trajectories empirically observable over time. While prior DSR research has emphasized ensemble artifacts, reciprocal shaping, and strategic evaluation, it still lacks a clear concept for artifacts whose incompleteness persists into operation. This paper introduces the concept of living artifacts to describe digital artifacts that remain incomplete after deployment, evolve in use, and are continuously evaluated through their digital traces.
